Exotic Hopf maps, weight shifting and applications to vector bundles

Jean Fasel ††thanks: Jean Fasel was partially supported by the project IRGA2024 –MOTOR – G7H-IRG24E97.    William Hornslien ††thanks: William Hornslien was partially supported by the project IRGA2024 –MOTOR – G7H-IRG24E97.
Abstract

Using motivic homotopy theory we produce several explicit polynomial representatives of the suspension of the Hopf map defined over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. We derive from this computation an explicit rank 22 vector bundle on the Jouanolou device of ℙℤ3\mathbb{P}^{3}_{\mathbb{Z}}.

1 Introduction

This paper can be viewed as an explicit version of some results in [2], where the problem of producing complex polynomial representatives of homotopy groups of spheres was considered. Recall that P. Baum proved in [13] that any element of the stable homotopy groups of spheres can be represented by an admissible quadratic map, i.e., a real polynomial map of degree at most 22. However, Wood later observed [28] that there are no non-constant polynomial maps Sn→SmS^{n}\to S^{m} for n≥2​mn\geq 2m, showing that Baum’s result fails in the unstable range. This led to the study of complex polynomial representatives, using the fact that the complex algebraic sphere SℂnS_{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, viewed as a manifold, is homotopy equivalent to the real sphere SnS^{n}. At present, no element of a homotopy group of spheres is known that cannot be represented by such a complex polynomial map.

In [2, Proposition 2.2.1], it was shown that the suspension of the Hopf map S4→S3S^{4}\to S^{3} and the square of the Hopf map S5→S3S^{5}\to S^{3} admit complex polynomial representatives. The method relied on motivic homotopy theory and a weight-shifting procedure that we briefly recall. If kk is a field and n≥1n\geq 1, consider the smooth quadrics Q2​n−1:={∑xiyi=1}⊂𝔸k2​nQ_{2n-1}:=\{\sum x_{i}y_{i}=1\}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2n}_{k} (with coordinates x1,…,xn,y1,…,ynx_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) and Q2​n:={∑xiyi=z(1−z)}⊂𝔸k2​n+1Q_{2n}:=\{\sum x_{i}y_{i}=z(1-z)\}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2n+1}_{k} (with coordinates x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn,zx_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},z). It is well known (e.g. [1]) that these quadrics model motivic spheres in the (unstable) motivic homotopy category ℋ⁡(k)\mathcal{H}(k) of Morel–Voevodsky [22]. Moreover, for any smooth affine kk-scheme XX, the map HomSchk​(X,Qi)→[X,Qi]𝔸1:=Homℋ⁡(k)​(X,Qi)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Sch}_{k}}(X,Q_{i})\to[X,Q_{i}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}:=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{H}(k)}(X,Q_{i}) is surjective for i≥1i\geq 1 ([9, Theorem 4.2.1], [10, Corollary 3.1.1]).

If k⊂ℂk\subset{\mathbb{C}}, the complex realization functor [22, §3.3]

rℂ:ℋ⁡(ℂ)→ℋr_{{\mathbb{C}}}\colon\mathcal{H}({\mathbb{C}})\to\mathcal{H}

(left Kan extended from X↦X⁡(ℂ)X\mapsto X({\mathbb{C}}) endowed with the complex topology) sends QiQ_{i} to SiS^{i}. Hence, we obtain a composite map

HomSchk​(Qj,Qi)→[Qj,Qi]𝔸1→πj​(Si)\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Sch}_{k}}(Q_{j},Q_{i})\to[Q_{j},Q_{i}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\to\pi_{j}(S^{i})

for any i,j≥1i,j\geq 1. Thus, to show that α∈πj​(Si)\alpha\in\pi_{j}(S^{i}) admits a polynomial representative, it suffices to produce a lift α′∈[Qj,Qi]𝔸1\alpha^{\prime}\in[Q_{j},Q_{i}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}. Since QjQ_{j} is a motivic sphere, we have identifications with bi-graded homotopy groups

[Qj,Qi]𝔸1={𝝅n,n𝔸1​(Qi)​(k) if j=2​n, 𝝅n−1,n𝔸1​(Qi)​(k) if j=2​n−1. [Q_{j},Q_{i}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}=\begin{cases}{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{n,n}(Q_{i})(k)&\text{ if $j=2n$, }\\ {\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{n-1,n}(Q_{i})(k)&\text{ if $j=2n-1$. }\end{cases}

These groups can sometimes be computed using fiber sequences analogous to those in topology. For example, setting i=3,j=4i=3,j=4 yields

𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Q3)=𝝅2,2𝔸1​(SL2)=𝝅2,2𝔸1​(𝔸2∖{0}),{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3})={\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(\mathrm{SL}_{2})={\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\}),

which fits in an exact sequence ([4, Theorem 3.3, Proposition 4.4])

𝐊2M(k)/12×𝐊2M​(k)/2𝐈2(k)→𝝅2,2𝔸1(Q3)(k)→𝐆𝐖10(k)→0.{{\mathbf{K}}_{2}^{\mathrm{M}}}(k)/12\times_{{{\mathbf{K}}_{2}^{\mathrm{M}}}(k)/2}\mathbf{I}^{2}(k)\to{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3})(k)\to\mathbf{GW}_{1}^{0}(k)\to 0.

If kk has characteristic ≠2\neq 2, then 𝐆𝐖10​(k)=KO1​(k)≃ℤ/2×k×/(k×)2\mathbf{GW}_{1}^{0}(k)=\mathrm{KO}_{1}(k)\simeq{\mathbb{Z}}/2\times k^{\times}/(k^{\times})^{2}. When k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, we obtain in particular 𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Q3)​(ℂ)≃ℤ/2{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3})({\mathbb{C}})\simeq{\mathbb{Z}}/2, and the generator maps to the generator of π4​(S3)=ℤ/2\pi_{4}(S^{3})={\mathbb{Z}}/2, namely the suspension of the Hopf map.

In [2], a different approach called weight shifting was used to produce a motivic lift of the suspension of the Hopf map. We observe that 𝝅1,3𝔸1​(Q3)=𝐖{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{1,3}(Q_{3})=\mathbf{W} (the Witt sheaf) and that its generator, as a 𝐊0MW{{\mathbf{K}}_{0}^{\mathrm{MW}}}-module, is 2ϵ2_{\epsilon}-torsion (with 2ϵ=⟨1,−1⟩∈GW⁡(k)2_{\epsilon}=\langle 1,-1\rangle\in\mathrm{GW}(k)). It is shown in [2, Theorem 2.1.11] that choosing −1-1 as a primitive 22nd root of unity induces a morphism of sheaves

𝐖=𝝅1,3𝔸12ϵ​(Q3)→𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Q3)/[−1]​𝝅2,3𝔸1​(Q3).\mathbf{W}={}_{2_{\epsilon}}{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{1,3}(Q_{3})\to{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3})/[-1]{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,3}(Q_{3}).

By construction, the image of the generator realizes to the suspension of the Hopf map. Although conceptually natural, this construction is difficult to make explicit and a geometric realization was missing.

In this article we give two explicit constructions of morphisms of quadrics Q4→Q3Q_{4}\to Q_{3}, called exotic Hopf maps, whose complex realization is the suspension of the Hopf map. The first construction uses the computation of 𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Q3){\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3}) above, specifically the morphism 𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Q3)→𝐆𝐖10​(k){\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3})\to\mathbf{GW}_{1}^{0}(k) and the summand ℤ/2⊂GW10​(k){\mathbb{Z}}/2\subset\mathrm{GW}_{1}^{0}(k). We first note that GW10​(k)=𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Sp)\mathrm{GW}_{1}^{0}(k)={\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(\mathrm{Sp}), where Sp\mathrm{Sp} denotes the infinite symplectic group defined over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. Hence

𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Sp)=[Q4,Sp]𝔸1=GW12​(Q4)=KSp1​(Q4).{\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(\mathrm{Sp})=[Q_{4},\mathrm{Sp}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}=\mathrm{GW}_{1}^{2}(Q_{4})=\mathrm{KSp}_{1}(Q_{4}).

Using the edge map in the coniveau spectral sequence for Hermitian KK-theory, we construct an explicit symplectic matrix M∈Sp8​(Q4)M\in\mathrm{Sp}_{8}(Q_{4}) representing the generator of ℤ/2{\mathbb{Z}}/2. Connectivity arguments show that this matrix can be reduced by elementary symplectic operations, although carrying this out explicitly is somewhat delicate. Nevertheless, we obtain the following theorem.

The second construction uses the weight-shifting procedure. Starting from the universal rank 22 bundle on Q5≃𝔸3∖0Q_{5}\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{3}\smallsetminus{0} classified by a map Q5→BSL2Q_{5}\to\mathrm{BSL}_{2}, adjunction yields a map S1,3→SL2=Q3S^{1,3}\to\mathrm{SL}_{2}=Q_{3}. Since S1,3S^{1,3} has no convenient model as a smooth scheme, we instead use a presentation as a quotient of Q3×𝔾mQ_{3}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{} (as Nisnevich sheaves of sets). This leads to a morphism of schemes

T:Q3×𝔾m→SL2=Q3T\colon Q_{3}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}\to\mathrm{SL}_{2}=Q_{3}

which is trivial on Q3∨𝔾mQ_{3}\vee{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}. Considering a model of the multiplication-by-22 map m′:Q3→Q3m^{\prime}\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{3}, one checks that the composite

Q3×𝔾m→m′×1Q3×𝔾m→Q3Q_{3}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}\xrightarrow{m^{\prime}\times 1}Q_{3}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}\to Q_{3}

is homotopically trivial. This produces a morphism

ϕ:Q3×𝔾m×𝔸1→Q3\phi\colon Q_{3}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to Q_{3}

with ϕ⁡(0)=Id\phi(0)=\mathrm{Id} and ϕ⁡(1)=T∘m′\phi(1)=T\circ m^{\prime}. Evaluating at the point −1∈𝔾m-1\in{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{} gives a morphism G:Q3×𝔸1→Q3G\colon Q_{3}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to Q_{3} satisfying G⁡(0)=G⁡(1)=IdG(0)=G(1)=\mathrm{Id} and then a map (Q3×𝔸1)/(Q3×S0)→Q3(Q_{3}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1})/(Q_{3}\times S^{0})\to Q_{3}. The source formally resembles a suspension of Q3Q_{3}, hence Q4Q_{4}. After suitable modifications and using a morphism Q3×(𝔸1∖{0,1})→Q4Q_{3}\times({\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1\})\to Q_{4} constructed in Section 2.1, we obtain the desired morphism Q4→Q3Q_{4}\to Q_{3}. At present we do not know whether the maps in Theorems 1 and 2 are homotopic over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. Both reduce to the identity over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}, since the generator of GW10​(k)\mathrm{GW}_{1}^{0}(k) in the first construction and −1-1 in the second become trivial modulo 22. −y12​i+4​y1​y2​i−y22​i−6​z2​i+i.\displaystyle-y_{1}^{2}i+4y_{1}y_{2}i-y_{2}^{2}i-6z^{2}i+i.

In Section 2.5, we develop a method for ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspending maps between quadrics. Given a map f∈HomSchk⁡(Qi,Qj)f\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Sch}_{k}}(Q_{i},Q_{j}), we produce a new map in HomSchk⁡(Qi+2,Qj+2)\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Sch}_{k}}(Q_{i+2},Q_{j+2}) which has the homotopy class of Σℙ1​f\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}f. We use this to give a procedure for constructing a map representing any homotopy class in [Qi,Qi]𝔸1≅GW⁡(k)[Q_{i},Q_{i}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\cong\mathrm{GW}(k) for i≥3i\geq 3.

In the second part of the paper, we apply our construction of the exotic Hopf map to obtain an explicit rank 22 vector bundle on a convenient replacement of ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. For context, recall that Atiyah and Rees observed in [11] that the bundle coming from the composite

ℂ​ℙ3→S6→Σ3​ηS5→B​U​(2){\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{3}\to S^{6}\xrightarrow{\Sigma^{3}\eta}S^{5}\to BU(2)

had trivial Chern classes, but was indecomposable. They then showed that all topological bundles on ℂ​ℙ3{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{3} are uniquely determined by their Chern classes and a ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}-invariant they called the α\alpha-invariant. Horrocks [20] came up with a way of constructing rank 22 bundles on ℂ​ℙ3{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{3} and Atiyah and Rees proved that all complex rank 22 topological vector bundles on ℂ​ℙ3{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{3} can be obtained by starting with a sum of line bundles and then iteratively tensoring with a line bundle and applying Horrocks’ construction [11, Theorem 1.1]. In [2], it was shown that the same story holds in (unstable) motivic homotopy theory. Namely, there is a composite

ℙk3→(ℙk1)∧3→Σℙ1​η′𝔸k3∖{0}→BSL2{\mathbb{P}}^{3}_{k}\to({\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{k})^{\wedge 3}\xrightarrow{\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\eta^{\prime}}{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{k}\smallsetminus\{0\}\to\mathrm{BSL}_{2}

where the first map is the “clutching” map, the second one is the class of any of the exotic Hopf maps constructed above and the third one is the map classifying the universal rank 22 bundle on 𝔸k3∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{k}\smallsetminus\{0\}. However, by construction this composite yields a class in [ℙk3,BSL2]𝔸1[{\mathbb{P}}^{3}_{k},\mathrm{BSL}_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}, i.e., a motivic vector bundle on ℙk3\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k}. Such a bundle can be seen as an actual algebraic vector bundle on a convenient affine replacement of ℙk3\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k}, the so-called Jouanolou device of ℙk3\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k} denoted by 𝕁k3\mathbb{J}^{3}_{k} below. Up to homotopy, the above composite then reads as

𝕁k3→Q6→Σℙ1​η′Q5→BSL2\mathbb{J}^{3}_{k}\to Q_{6}\xrightarrow{\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\eta^{\prime}}Q_{5}\to\mathrm{BSL}_{2}

where the first map is an explicit model of the clutching map provided in Section 2.4 below, and the results in the first part of the paper allow us to obtain an explicit idempotent 3×33\times 3-matrix of rank 22 on 𝕁k3\mathbb{J}^{3}_{k} that is the algebraic construction of the topological composite above. If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, we prove that it has the expected algebraic invariants: trivial Chern classes and non-trivial Atiyah-Rees invariant. In view of Horrock’s construction, the vector bundle on 𝕁k3\mathbb{J}^{3}_{k} is pulled-back from ℙk3{\mathbb{P}}^{3}_{k} in case k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, but we don’t know if this is the case over an arbitrary field.

Conventions

We work over a perfect field kk. We use the conventions of [2] for motivic homotopy theory, and the notation of [6, §3] for higher Grothendieck-Witt sheaves (a.k.a. Hermitian KK-theory sheaves). In particular, we will use symplectic KK-theory and denote the usual skew-symmetric matrix on ℤ2{\mathbb{Z}}^{2} by HH, i.e.,

H:=(01−10).H:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}.

2 Maps between quadrics

2.1 Basics on quadrics

We start by exploring a bit the geometry of Q2​nQ_{2n} for n≥1n\geq 1. Recall first from [7, §2.1] that a morphism from an affine kk-scheme X=Spec⁡(R)X=\mathrm{Spec}(R) to Q2​nQ_{2n} is determined up to homotopy by an ideal I:=⟨a1,…,an,s⟩⊂RI:=\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},s\rangle\subset R such that I/I2I/I^{2} is generated by the classes of a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}. Using this, one sees that s−s2∈⟨a1,…,an⟩s-s^{2}\in\langle a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\rangle, i.e. there exists b1,…,bn∈Rb_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in R such that s⁡(1−s)=∑i=1nai​bis(1-s)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i} and two choices of b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n} are homotopic. Granted this, we will mostly define morphisms to Q2​nQ_{2n} using explicit descriptions of ideals.

We consider the closed subschemes

Z0:={x1=…=xn=z=0}⊂Q2​n,Z1:={x1=…=xn=1−z=0}⊂Q2​nZ_{0}:=\{x_{1}=\ldots=x_{n}=z=0\}\subset Q_{2n},\phantom{i}Z_{1}:=\{x_{1}=\ldots=x_{n}=1-z=0\}\subset Q_{2n}

and set Xi:=Q2​n∖ZiX_{i}:=Q_{2n}\smallsetminus Z_{i} for i=0,1i=0,1. It is straightforward to check that Zi≃𝔸nZ_{i}\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{n} (with coordinates y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) and we know from [1, Theorem 3.1.1] that the subschemes XiX_{i} are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. On the other hand

X0∩X1=Q2​n∖(Z0⊔Z1)=Q2​n∖{x1=…=xn=0}X_{0}\cap X_{1}=Q_{2n}\smallsetminus(Z_{0}\sqcup Z_{1})=Q_{2n}\smallsetminus\{x_{1}=\ldots=x_{n}=0\}

and there is an obvious projection morphism

pn:X0∩X1→𝔸n∖{0},(x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn,z)↦(x1,…,xn).p_{n}\colon X_{0}\cap X_{1}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\},\phantom{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},z)\mapsto(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}).
Lemma 2.1.1.

The map pn:X0∩X1→𝔸n∖{0}p_{n}\colon X_{0}\cap X_{1}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\} is a weak equivalence.

Proof.

We can cover 𝔸n∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\} by the open subschemes D(xi)={xi≠0}⊂𝔸n∖{0}D(x_{i})=\{x_{i}\neq 0\}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\}. The preimage of D⁡(xi)D(x_{i}) under pnp_{n} is an affine space over D⁡(xi)D(x_{i}) with coordinates y1,…,yi−1,yi+1,…,yn,zy_{1},\ldots,y_{i-1},y_{i+1},\ldots,y_{n},z. ∎

We can construct an inverse (up to homotopy) of that map, using the morphism

αn:Q2​n−1×𝔸1→Q2​n\alpha_{n}\colon Q_{2n-1}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to Q_{2n}

given on coordinates by (x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn,t)↦(x1,…,xn,y1​t​(1−t),…,yn​t​(1−t),t)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},t)\mapsto(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1}t(1-t),\ldots,y_{n}t(1-t),t). A direct computation shows that it factors through X0∩X1X_{0}\cap X_{1}, and that the composite

Q2​n−1×𝔸1→αnX0∩X1→pn𝔸n∖{0}Q_{2n-1}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\xrightarrow{\alpha_{n}}X_{0}\cap X_{1}\xrightarrow{p_{n}}{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\}

is just the projection map (which is a weak-equivalence). For further use, we also note that αn\alpha_{n} induces an isomorphism

αn:Q2​n−1×(𝔸1∖{0,1})≃D⁡(z⁡(1−z))⊂Q2​n\alpha_{n}\colon Q_{2n-1}\times({\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1\})\simeq D(z(1-z))\subset Q_{2n}

with inverse given (x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn,z)↦(x1,…,xn,y1z⁡(1−z),…,ynz⁡(1−z),z)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},z)\mapsto(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\frac{y_{1}}{z(1-z)},\ldots,\frac{y_{n}}{z(1-z)},z).

2.3 The Jouanolou device of ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}

Recall that the usual Jouanolou device 𝕁n\mathbb{J}^{n} of ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n} is given by the functor associating to a kk-algebra RR the set of matrices P∈Mn+1​(R)P\in M_{n+1}(R) of rank one satisfying P2=PP^{2}=P. We have an explicit presentation of the algebra representing this functor via

k[𝕁n]=k[xi​j|1≤i,j≤n+1]/(xi​j=∑r=1n+1xi​rxr​j∀1≤i,j≤n+1,D)k[\mathbb{J}^{n}]=k[x_{ij}|1\leq i,j\leq n+1]/\left(x_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^{n+1}x_{ir}x_{rj}\forall 1\leq i,j\leq n+1,D\right)

where DD is the set of all 2×22\times 2 minors of PP. There is a universal matrix P=(xi​j)P=(x_{ij}) on k⁡[𝕁n]k[\mathbb{J}^{n}] which satisfies P2=PP^{2}=P by the first set of equations. This yields a projector PRP_{R} on Rn+1R^{n+1} for any homomorphism of kk-algebras k⁡[𝕁n]→Rk[\mathbb{J}^{n}]\to R and we set L=Im⁡(P)⊂Rn+1L=\mathrm{Im}(P)\subset R^{n+1}. This is a projective module and we can compute its rank by considering residue fields of RR. If FF is a field we know that the matrix PFP_{F} satisfies PF2=PFP^{2}_{F}=P_{F} and it follows in particular that PFP_{F} is diagonalizable with possible eigenvalues 00 and 11. The condition on the minors forces PFP_{F} to be of rank one, and consequently LL is of rank one as required.

Remark 2.3.1.

If kk is of characteristic 00, we can replace the conditions D=0D=0 by the easier condition ∑i=1n+1xi​i=1\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}x_{ii}=1, i.e. the matrix is of trace 11.

We have an obvious morphism of schemes

p:𝕁n→ℙnp:\mathbb{J}^{n}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{n}

corresponding to the line bundle LL and its generating sections given by k​[𝕁n]n+1→𝑃Lk[\mathbb{J}^{n}]^{n+1}\xrightarrow{P}L. pi:Ui→𝔸np_{i}:U_{i}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}

2.5 An explicit ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspension map of maps between quadrics

In this section, we provide an explicit way of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspending morphisms of quadrics, starting with the following observation: For n≥1n\geq 1, consider 𝔸2​n+2{\mathbb{A}}^{2n+2} with variables x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn,t,ux_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},t,u. We have fn:=∑i=1nxi​yi−1f_{n}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}-1 and g=t​u−1g=tu-1. These polynomials are irreducible, hence prime in k⁡[𝔸2​n+2]k[{\mathbb{A}}^{2n+2}], and

V⁡(fn)=Q2​n−1×𝔸2,V⁡(g)=𝔸2​n×𝔾m.V(f_{n})=Q_{2n-1}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2},\phantom{i}V(g)={\mathbb{A}}^{2n}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}.

where X2​n+1=V⁡(fn⋅g)⊂𝔸2​n+2X_{2n+1}=V(f_{n}\cdot g)\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2n+2}. 2.6 Endomorphisms of quadrics of arbitrary 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-Brouwer degree

In this section we give a procedure for constructing morphisms Qn→QnQ_{n}\to Q_{n} representing each element in GW⁡(k)\mathrm{GW}(k), for n≥2n\geq 2 (stably if n=2n=2). We begin by constructing the morphisms in the cases [Q2,Q2]𝔸1[Q_{2},Q_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} and [Q3,Q3]𝔸1[Q_{3},Q_{3}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} and then suspend accordingly using Lemmas 2.5.2 and 2.5.1. We start with considering endomorphisms of Q3Q_{3}.

Lemma 2.6.1.

The map Q3→Q3Q_{3}\to Q_{3} given by the unimodular row (x1,u​x2)(x_{1},ux_{2}) represents the class ⟨u⟩∈GW⁡(k)\langle u\rangle\in\mathrm{GW}(k) and the row (y1,−u​x2)(y_{1},-ux_{2}) represents the class −⟨u⟩∈GW⁡(k)-\langle u\rangle\in\mathrm{GW}(k)

Proof.

For a unit u∈k×u\in k^{\times}, the map 𝔸2∖{0}→𝔸2∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\} given on coordinates by (x1,x2)↦(x1,u​x2)(x_{1},x_{2})\mapsto(x_{1},ux_{2}) has 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-Brouwer degree ⟨u⟩\langle u\rangle [21, Lemma 9]. Since Q3≃𝔸2∖{0}Q_{3}\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\}, this endomorphism lifts to the map Q3→Q3Q_{3}\to Q_{3} given by the SL2​(k​[Q3])\mathrm{SL}_{2}(k[Q_{3}])-matrix.

mu=(x1u​x2−u−1​y2y1).m_{u}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}&ux_{2}\\ -u^{-1}y_{2}&y_{1}\end{pmatrix}.

The group structure on [Q3,Q3]𝔸1[Q_{3},Q_{3}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} is given by the group structure on SL2\mathrm{SL}_{2}, hence the morphism representing −⟨u⟩-\langle u\rangle is given by the inverse matrix

mu−1=(x1u​x2−u−1​y2y1)−1=(y1−u​x2u−1​y2x1).m_{u}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}&ux_{2}\\ -u^{-1}y_{2}&y_{1}\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}y_{1}&-ux_{2}\\ u^{-1}y_{2}&x_{1}\end{pmatrix}.

∎

Given an element in q∈GW⁡(k)q\in\mathrm{GW}(k), one does the following to find a morphism Q3→Q3Q_{3}\to Q_{3} with 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-Brouwer degree qq:

  1. 1.

    Write qq as a sum q=⟨u1,…,ur⟩−⟨v1,…,vs⟩q=\langle u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}\rangle-\langle v_{1},\ldots,v_{s}\rangle.

  2. 2.

    Compute the matrix product Mq=mu1​…​mur​mv1−1​…​mvs−1.M_{q}=m_{u_{1}}\ldots m_{u_{r}}m_{v_{1}}^{-1}\ldots m_{v_{s}}^{-1}.

  3. 3.

    The first row of MqM_{q} is a unimodular row with 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-Brouwer degree q.q.

We will now consider Q2Q_{2}-endomorphisms. Note that Q2≃𝕁1≃ℙ1Q_{2}\simeq\mathbb{J}^{1}\simeq{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and that in [12] the group structure on [Q2,ℙ1]𝔸1[Q_{2},{\mathbb{P}}^{1}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} is studied. The first complication is that [Q2,Q2]𝔸1[Q_{2},Q_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} is not in the stable range, and we have [Q2,Q2]𝔸1≅GW⁡(k)×k×/k×2k×[Q_{2},Q_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\cong\mathrm{GW}(k)\times_{k^{\times}/k^{\times 2}}k^{\times}, but under stabilization, this map is just projection onto GW⁡(k)\mathrm{GW}(k) (use for instance [23, Theorem 6.37]. The group operation on [Q2,ℙ1]𝔸1[Q_{2},{\mathbb{P}}^{1}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} is in general not easy to describe, but the operation of adding a rank 00 map to any other map can be described easily. We first begin by describing the generators of the rank 00 maps. For u∈k×u\in k^{\times}, we denote by fu:Q2→Q2f_{u}\colon Q_{2}\to Q_{2} the morphism given by the ideal ⟨u​x1,z⟩\langle ux_{1},z\rangle.

Lemma 2.6.2.

Let u,v∈k×u,v\in k^{\times}, then the stable class of the morphism fu,v:Q2→Q2f_{u,v}\colon Q_{2}\to Q_{2} given by the ideal ⟨(u−v)u​v​x1,z+vu​(1−z)⟩\langle\frac{(u-v)}{uv}x_{1},z+\frac{v}{u}(1-z)\rangle is ⟨u⟩−⟨v⟩\langle u\rangle-\langle v\rangle.

Proof.

It follows from [12, Proposition 103] that the stable class of fuf_{u} is ⟨u⟩\langle u\rangle, and from [12, Lemma 91] that the class of fu,v⊕fvf_{u,v}\oplus f_{v} is ⟨u⟩\langle u\rangle. Hence the class of fu,vf_{u,v} is ⟨u⟩−⟨v⟩\langle u\rangle-\langle v\rangle. ∎

Since all Q2Q_{2}-endomorphisms representing rank 00 forms factor through Q3Q_{3} ([12, Corollary 43]), the ideal described in Lemma 2.6.2 is in fact a unimodular row. Thus we define the SL2​(k​[Q2])\mathrm{SL_{2}}(k[Q_{2}])-matrix

mu,v:=(z+vu​(1−z)(u−v)u​v​x1(u−v)​y1z+uv​(1−z)).m_{u,v}:=\begin{pmatrix}z+\frac{v}{u}(1-z)&\frac{(u-v)}{uv}x_{1}\\ (u-v)y_{1}&z+\frac{u}{v}(1-z)\end{pmatrix}.

Consider polynomials An​(z),Bn​(z)A_{n}(z),B_{n}(z) defined such that (z+(1−z))2​n=zn​An​(z)+(1−z)n​Bn​(z)(z+(1-z))^{2n}=z^{n}A_{n}(z)+(1-z)^{n}B_{n}(z).

Lemma 2.6.3.

Let n>0n>0 then:

  1. 1.

    The map Q2→Q2Q_{2}\to Q_{2} given by the ideal ⟨zn​A​(n),x1n​An​(z)⟩\langle z^{n}A(n),x_{1}^{n}A_{n}(z)\rangle has degree n2​⟨1,−1⟩\frac{n}{2}\langle 1,-1\rangle when nn is even and n−12​⟨1,−1⟩+⟨1⟩\frac{n-1}{2}\langle 1,-1\rangle+\langle 1\rangle when nn is odd.

  2. 2.

    The map Q2→Q2Q_{2}\to Q_{2} given by the ideal ⟨zn​An​(z),y1n​An​(z)⟩\langle z^{n}A_{n}(z),y_{1}^{n}A_{n}(z)\rangle has degree −n2​⟨1,−1⟩-\frac{n}{2}\langle 1,-1\rangle when nn is even and −n−12​⟨1,−1⟩−⟨−1⟩-\frac{n-1}{2}\langle 1,-1\rangle-\langle-1\rangle when nn is odd.

Proof.

Since these morphisms are defined over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}, one can use a similar argument as the proof of Theorem 105 in [12] to show that the class the morphisms are determined by the Brouwer degree of their real and complex realizations. ∎

A Q2Q_{2}-endomorphism can be described as a (2×2)(2\times 2) idempotent matrix PP with trace 11 and entries in k⁡[Q2]k[Q_{2}]. For n≥0n\geq 0, we define the idempotent matrices

Pn=(zn​An​(z)x1n​An​(z)y1n​Bn​(z)(1−z)n​Bn​(z))P−n=(zn​An​(z)y1n​An​(z)x1n​Bn​(z)(1−z)n​Bn​(z)).P_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}z^{n}A_{n}(z)&x_{1}^{n}A_{n}(z)\\ y_{1}^{n}B_{n}(z)&(1-z)^{n}B_{n}(z)\end{pmatrix}\quad P_{-n}=\begin{pmatrix}z^{n}A_{n}(z)&y_{1}^{n}A_{n}(z)\\ x_{1}^{n}B_{n}(z)&(1-z)^{n}B_{n}(z)\end{pmatrix}.

In loc.cit. an action of rank 00 maps on rank nn maps is described, and it is shown that this agrees with the group operation on [Q2,ℙ1]𝔸1[Q_{2},{\mathbb{P}}^{1}]^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}. One can check, following Remark 84 loc.cit, that the action of mu,vm_{u,v} on PP is given by the matrix mu,v​P​mu,v−1m_{u,v}Pm_{u,v}^{-1}.

Given an element in q∈GW⁡(k)q\in\mathrm{GW}(k), one does the following to find a morphism Q2→Q2Q_{2}\to Q_{2} that stably represents qq.

If qq is of odd rank nn, write it as a sum n−12​⟨1,−1⟩+⟨1⟩+∑i=1r⟨ui⟩−⟨vi⟩\frac{n-1}{2}\langle 1,-1\rangle+\langle 1\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\langle u_{i}\rangle-\langle v_{i}\rangle for some units ui,vi∈k×u_{i},v_{i}\in k^{\times}.

Remark 2.6.4.

The reason we do not decompose qq as a sum n⁡⟨1⟩+∑i=1m⟨ui⟩−⟨vi⟩n\langle 1\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\langle u_{i}\rangle-\langle v_{i}\rangle is that the Q2Q_{2}-endomorphism representing n​⟨1⟩n\langle 1\rangle is a lot more complicated to write down compared to the maps given in Lemma 2.6.3.

2.7 Motivic Hopf maps

Given an H-space XX, the Hopf construction detailed in [23, §7.3] provides us with a fiber sequence

X→X⋆X→Σ​X.X\to X\star X\to\Sigma X.

Applying this to the algebraic group 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} yields the fiber sequence

𝔾m→Q3→Q2.{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{}\to Q_{3}\to Q_{2}.

The map η:Q3→Q2\eta\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{2} can be described as the rank 11 projective k⁡[Q3]k[Q_{3}]-module

(x1​y1x2​y1x1​y2x2​y2).\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}y_{1}&x_{2}y_{1}\\ x_{1}y_{2}&x_{2}y_{2}\end{pmatrix}.
Proposition 2.7.1.

The map f:Q3→Q2f\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{2} defined by (x1,x2,y1,y2)↦(x2​y1,x1​y2,x1​y1)(x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2})\mapsto(x_{2}y_{1},x_{1}y_{2},x_{1}y_{1}) represents the Hopf map. For n≥2n\geq 2, the map f:Q2​n+1→Q2​nf\colon Q_{2n+1}\to Q_{2n} defined by mapping (x1,x2,…,xn+1,y1,y2,…,yn+1)(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n+1},y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n+1}) to (x2​y1,x3,…,xn+1,x1​y2,y3​x1​y1,…,yn+1​x1​y1,x1​y1)(x_{2}y_{1},x_{3},\ldots,x_{n+1},x_{1}y_{2},y_{3}x_{1}y_{1},\ldots,y_{n+1}x_{1}y_{1},x_{1}y_{1}) is the (n−1)(n-1)-fold ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-suspension of the Hopf map η:Q3→Q2\eta\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{2}.

Proof.

For the first claim, recall that we have a homotopy equivalence π:Q3→𝔸2∖{0}\pi\colon Q_{3}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\} sending (x1,x2,y1,y2)(x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2}) to the point (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}) in 𝔸2∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\}. There is also a homotopy equivalence Q2→ℙ1Q_{2}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{1} which maps a point (x1,y1,z)∈Q2(x_{1},y_{1},z)\in Q_{2} to the point [z:x1][z:x_{1}] or [y1:1−z][y_{1}:1-z] (whichever is defined). The Hopf map η:𝔸2∖{0}→ℙ1\eta\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{0\}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{1} is defined by (x1,x2)→[x1:x2](x_{1},x_{2})\to[x_{1}:x_{2}]. It is straightforward to check that the square

commutes. The second claim then follows from Lemma 2.5.1. ∎

Remark 2.7.2.

We could instead consider the map g:Q3→Q2g\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{2} defined by

(x1,x2,y1,y2)↦(x1​x2,y1​y2,x2​y2),(x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2})\mapsto(x_{1}x_{2},y_{1}y_{2},x_{2}y_{2}),

which looks more symmetric (and could actually be used to obtain the so-called strong Euler class defined in [14] and [27]). It differs from the previous one by the automorphism a:Q3→Q3a\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{3} defined by x1↦y2,x2↦x1,y1↦x2,y2↦y1x_{1}\mapsto y_{2},x_{2}\mapsto x_{1},y_{1}\mapsto x_{2},y_{2}\mapsto y_{1}. Since

(y2x1−y1x2)=(x2−x1y1y2)−1​ and ​(x2−x1y1y2)=(x1x2−y2y1)​(0−110)\begin{pmatrix}y_{2}&x_{1}\\ -y_{1}&x_{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}&-x_{1}\\ y_{1}&y_{2}\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\text{ and }\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}&-x_{1}\\ y_{1}&y_{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}&x_{2}\\ -y_{2}&y_{1}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}

we see that the map g:Q3→Q2g\colon Q_{3}\to Q_{2} is homotopic to −η-\eta.

Using the Hopf construction for the algebraic group SL2\mathrm{SL}_{2} yields the fiber sequence

SL2→Q7→𝜈Q4.\mathrm{SL_{2}}\to Q_{7}\xrightarrow{\nu}Q_{4}.

As explained in [18, §3], the scheme Q7Q_{7} can be seen of the scheme of pairs of (2×2)(2\times 2)-matrices (M1,M2)(M_{1},M_{2}) with detM1+detM2=1\det M_{1}+\det M_{2}=1. The map ν:Q7→Q4\nu\colon Q_{7}\to Q_{4} is given by (M1​M2,det(M1))(M_{1}M_{2},\det(M_{1})), and its real realization is actually the Hopf map by [18, Proposition 3.0.1]. Note that the complex realization of ν\nu is the second Hopf map by [19]. Using once again Lemma 2.5.1, we obtain the following proposition.

Proposition 2.7.3.

Let n≥2n\geq 2. The map f:Q2​n+3→Q2​nf\colon Q_{2n+3}\to Q_{2n} defined by the ideal

(−x3​y1−x2​y4,−x4​y1+x2​y3,x5,…,xn+2,x3​y3+x4​y4)(-x_{3}y_{1}-x_{2}y_{4},-x_{4}y_{1}+x_{2}y_{3},x_{5},\ldots,x_{n+2},x_{3}y_{3}+x_{4}y_{4})

is the (n−2)(n-2)-fold ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-suspension of the Hopf map ν:Q7→Q4\nu\colon Q_{7}\to Q_{4}.

Complex realization of the maps from Proposition 2.7.1 gives us complex algebraic representatives of the maps Σ2​n−2​η\Sigma^{2n-2}\eta in the category of topological spaces. Similarly, the real realization of the maps from Proposition 2.7.3 gives us real algebraic representatives of the maps Σn−2​η\Sigma^{n-2}\eta. Our two families of maps do not allow us to create a map whose complex realization is Σ​η\Sigma\eta. Such a map would need to be a map Q4→Q3Q_{4}\to Q_{3}, and we construct such a map in the next section.

Remark 3.2.3.

We note that both the exotic Hopf maps obtained in Section 3.1 and above are defined over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. However, they reduce to a homotopically trivial map over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} as a direct check shows. In the second case, this can be explained by the fact that we had to choose a primitive 22nd root of 11. In the first case, we used a computation of GW10​(k)\mathrm{GW}_{1}^{0}(k) that needs 22 to be invertible, and the generator we used is trivial in GW10​(𝔽2)\mathrm{GW}_{1}^{0}(\mathbb{F}_{2}).

Remark 3.2.4.

A direct computation shows that the above map is not trivial relative z⁡(1−z)z(1-z). This could probably be further achieved by modifying it up to homotopy, but we haven’t carried out the necessary computations since we don’t need this property in the sequel.

Remark 3.2.5.

It would probably be difficult to prove that the exotic Hopf maps of Section 3.1 and the one above are homotopic. They however coincide after base change to ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, since [Q4,Q3]𝔸1=𝝅2,2𝔸1​(Q3)​(ℂ)≃ℤ/2[Q_{4},Q_{3}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}={\bm{\pi}}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}_{2,2}(Q_{3})({\mathbb{C}})\simeq{\mathbb{Z}}/2 and both maps are non-trivial (their complex realizations being non-trivial).

is an isomorphism. The same applies for ℙk2\mathbb{P}^{2}_{k} and thus the above diagram is of the form

By construction, the bundle constructed using the exotic Hopf map is classified by the composite

𝕁3→Q6→Σℙ1​η′Q5→BSL2\mathbb{J}^{3}\to Q_{6}\xrightarrow{\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\eta^{\prime}}Q_{5}\to\mathrm{BSL}_{2}

The sequence 𝕁3∖𝔸3→𝑖𝕁3→Q6\mathbb{J}^{3}\smallsetminus{\mathbb{A}}^{3}\xrightarrow{i}\mathbb{J}^{3}\to Q_{6} being isomorphic to the cofiber sequence

ℙk3∖{0}→ℙk3→(ℙ1)∧3\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k}\smallsetminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k}\to({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge 3}

we obtain that the composite 𝕁3∖𝔸3→𝑖𝕁3→Q6\mathbb{J}^{3}\smallsetminus{\mathbb{A}}^{3}\xrightarrow{i}\mathbb{J}^{3}\to Q_{6} is trivial up to homotopy. The diagram then shows in particular that the second Chern class of this bundle vanishes. We can now use the morphism ℙk3→(ℙ1)∧3\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k}\to({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge 3}, modeled by the morphism 𝕁3→Q6\mathbb{J}^{3}\to Q_{6}, to obtain a commutative diagram with exact columns

In view of [7, Proposition 1.1.5], the only nontrivial group in the top row is

H3​((ℙ1)∧3,𝐆𝐖32)=𝐆𝐖03​(k)=ℤ/2​ℤ,\mathrm{H}^{3}(({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge 3},\mathbf{GW}_{3}^{2})=\mathbf{GW}_{0}^{3}(k)={\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}},

and we thus obtain

We claim that he composite

ℤ/2=𝐆𝐖03​(k)=H3​((ℙ1)∧3,𝐆𝐖32)→H3​(ℙk3,𝐆𝐖32)→[ℙk3,BSL2]𝔸1{\mathbb{Z}}/2=\mathbf{GW}_{0}^{3}(k)=\mathrm{H}^{3}(({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge 3},\mathbf{GW}_{3}^{2})\to\mathrm{H}^{3}(\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k},\mathbf{GW}_{3}^{2})\to[\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k},\mathrm{BSL}_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}

is split injective.

Indeed, we consider the map [ℙk3,BSL2]𝔸1→[ℙk3,BSp]𝔸1=GW~2​(ℙk3)[\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k},\mathrm{BSL}_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\to[\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k},\mathrm{BSp}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}=\widetilde{\mathrm{GW}}^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{k}^{3}) induced by the stabilization, where the right-hand side is the reduced Grothendieck-Witt group of symplectic bundles. The push-forward map induced by the projection ℙk3→Spec⁡(k)\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k}\to\operatorname{Spec}(k) reads as

GW~2​(ℙk3)→GW3​(Spec⁡(k))=ℤ/2\widetilde{\mathrm{GW}}^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{k}^{3})\to\mathrm{GW}^{3}(\operatorname{Spec}(k))={\mathbb{Z}}/2

and is explicitly described in [3, §4.2.2], where it is called the motivic Atiyah-Rees invariant. The computation therein shows that this homomorphism provides a splitting of ℤ/2→[ℙk3,BSL2]𝔸1{\mathbb{Z}}/2\to[\mathbb{P}^{3}_{k},\mathrm{BSL}_{2}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}, and thus that the Atiyah-Rees invariant of the exotic Hopf bundle is 1∈ℤ/21\in{\mathbb{Z}}/2.
